1  Introduction
Vector-borne diseases continue to pose a significant public health threat in tropical and 
subtropical regions such as Vietnam, where arboviruses, including dengue, malaria, and 
Zika are transmitted by vectors such as Anopheles and Aedes species [1–3]. While the 
World Health Organization emphasizes the importance of environmental management 
and vector control [4], traditional field-based surveillance methods are often inefficient 
for large-scale and real-time monitoring [5]. UAVs offer a cost-effective alternative as 
they provide high-resolution images with greater spatial and temporal precision than 
Discover Artificial Intelligence
Abstract
Vector-borne diseases pose a persistent public health challenge in tropical regions 
such as Vietnam, where traditional ground-based surveillance methods struggle 
with scale and accuracy. This study presents a framework that integrates Unmanned 
Aerial Vehicle (UAV) multispectral imagery with deep learning techniques to detect 
small-to-medium-sized water bodies, important habitats for arbovirus vectors. 
High-resolution multispectral images were captured with the DJI Phantom 4 (P4M) 
Multispectral UAV in rural and peri-urban areas of Binh Duong province in Vietnam. A 
curated dataset of 982 annotated images was created, comprising RGB, near-infrared 
(NIR), and normalized difference water index (NDWI) bands. Six state-of-the-art object 
detection and segmentation models were evaluated, including YOLOv7, YOLOv7x, 
DocF, U-Net, MSNet, and RTFNet. Among them, segmentation models (U-Net and 
MSNet) using RGB + Green + NIR + NDWI achieved the best performance with dice 
scores above 0.92. The results show that the combination of UAV multispectral 
imagery with deep learning significantly improves the detection accuracy of water 
bodies in complex tropical conditions. This approach provides a scalable, cost-
effective solution for mapping small water bodies and contributes to targeted vector 
control and disease prevention measures in arbovirus-prone regions.
Keywords  UAV, Multispectral imagery, Water body detection, Arbovirus vector, Deep 
learning, Vietnam

satellite data [6], thus overcoming many limitations of conventional surveillance meth­
ods [7–9]. UAVs enable rapid detection of water bodies and other environmental fea­
tures linked to vector proliferation, significantly reducing the labour required for 
comprehensive monitoring efforts [10–15]. Both natural and artificial aquatic habitats 
such as swamps, streams, ponds, drainage ditches, and construction footprints serve as 
key breeding grounds for arbovirus vectors [16, 17].
Despite their potential, the use of UAVs for water body detection and vector habitat 
mapping in Vietnam remains limited. Dense vegetation cover, frequent cloudiness, and 
long rainy seasons hinder consistent data collection and reliable detection [18, 19]. A 
major constraint is the lack of high-quality multispectral datasets that capture small-to-
medium-sized water bodies in Vietnam’s urban and peri-urban tropical environments. 
Existing studies have demonstrated the utility of UAV multispectral imagery for water 
mapping and quality monitoring [20, 21], but they typically rely on proprietary datasets 
from non-tropical regions [22].
Conventional approaches to water body detection have relied primarily on natural-
colour (RGB) imagery [11–13]. While effective in some contexts, RGB lacks the spectral 
depth to distinguish water bodies from dense vegetation. Multispectral imagery, which 
includes Near-Infrared (NIR) and indices like the Normalized Difference Water Index 
(NDWI), enhances the ability to differentiate water from surrounding land cover, espe­
cially under complex environmental conditions [23]. This richer spectral information 
allows for finer detection of small or obscured aquatic features such as ponds or roadside 
puddles in rural and peri-urban landscapes [12, 14, 15, 23]. Traditional machine learning 
methods, such as Random Forests, have been applied in this domain [15, 24] but often 
struggle to scale or generalise in complex tropical environments. Issues such as dense 
canopies and fluctuating weather conditions further compromise the quality of multi­
spectral data. These limitations call for deep learning techniques capable of leveraging 
multispectral information to accurately detect water bodies and support precise vector 
habitat mapping.
This study addresses key challenges by pursuing several objectives. First, it aims to 
develop a UAV multispectral framework for detecting small-to-medium-sized aquatic 
habitats that serve as breeding grounds for arbovirus vectors. It also seeks to construct 
a customised multispectral dataset encompassing urban and peri-urban environments, 
including orthomosaics, raw spectral bands, and pixel-level annotations. To enhance 
water body detection in tropical conditions, the study combines spectral bands, spe­
cifically RGB, NIR, and NDWI. Finally, it trains and evaluates six deep learning mod­
els—YOLOv7, YOLOv7x, DocF, U-Net, MSNet, and RTFNet—for multi-class object 
detection using various band combinations.

3  Phase 1: Study design and data collection
The study was conducted in the town of Ben Cat, located in Binh Duong Province, where 
the population is particularly vulnerable to arboviral diseases. The study site was chosen 
for its diverse range of water bodies, including reservoirs, ponds, temporary pools, and 
road puddles found across rural and peri-urban settings. A detailed map of the study 
areas is presented in Fig. 2. The area encompasses Ben Cat and its surrounding regions 
within a radius of approximately 9 km. This includes the Vietnamese German University 
campus and two residential zones near Thoi Hoa, along with ten survey sites in An Dien 
(11.1348° N, 106.50702° E; population: 4), each separated by a radius of 8.7 km. While 
the university campus and the residential area in Thoi Hoa are densely populated, An 
Dien is characterised by rice fields and represents a more rural environment.

We employed the DJI Phantom 4 Multispectral (P4M) UAV along with DJI GS Pro 
software for image acquisition. The UAV and its multispectral camera system are shown 
in Fig. 2. The UAV is equipped with a high-quality multispectral imaging system that 
includes five spectral bands: Red, Green, Blue, Near-Infrared (NIR), and Red-edge. Inte­
gration with a Real-Time Kinematics (RTK) system ensures highly accurate positioning, 
optimising both automated flight planning and control processes. DJI GS Pro played a 
crucial role in efficient flight management and precise multispectral image acquisition, 
contributing to accurate mapping and data collection.
Before each flight, spectral calibration was performed using MicaSense Calibrated 
Reflectance Panels. Post-flight, the images were further calibrated to enhance spectral 
accuracy and ensure optimal brightness. Flight paths were carefully planned to maintain 
consistency across image captures, with data collection carried out between August and 
November 2023, during the rainy season and under wet weather conditions. A total of 
16 flight sessions were conducted to ensure uniformity across consecutive image sets.
To support model training, a comprehensive strategy was adopted for the acquisition 
and annotation of images. Each image covered an area of approximately 100 × 100 m or 
200 × 200 m (equivalent to 4 hectares), captured at a flight speed of 5 m/s and an alti­
tude of 120 m above ground level. The study design ensured approximately 70% overlap 
between images to support the generation of orthomosaic maps.
4  Phase 2: Image preprocessing
The final dataset consisted of 982 images across five spectral bands: RGB, NIR, and Red 
Edge, with each image having a resolution of 1600 × 1300 pixels. Representative exam­
ples of RGB and NIR images from the multispectral UAV dataset are shown in Fig. 3. 
The RGB images, composed of three 8-bit channels (Red, Green, and Blue), were used 
exclusively for training RGB-based models. In contrast, the Near-Infrared (NIR) band, 
captured by the P4M camera, was essential for training multispectral models. To further 
enrich the spectral information, the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) was 
computed as described in the experimental setup section.
To ensure high dataset quality, images compromised by poor weather conditions, 
such as darkness or heavy cloud cover were filtered out, as these factors hinder accurate 
manual annotation. The RGB bands span the visible spectrum from approximately 450–
590 nm, capturing key variations in colour and brightness for effective land cover dis­
crimination. The NIR band, centred at 790 nm, leverages the strong absorption of water 
and high reflectance of vegetation to enhance the contrast between aquatic features 
and surrounding land. The dataset’s spatial resolutions, 0.0265 m/pixel and 0.0353 m/
pixel, offer sub-decimetre detail, allowing precise delineation of small water bodies while 
maintaining manageable data sizes for model inference. The spectral specifications of 
each output folder are detailed in Table 1.
Pix4Dmapper was used to process the UAV-captured images and generate high-reso­
lution orthomosaic images. The raw images were first imported into Pix4Dmapper with 
key configurations, including the use of the WGS 84 coordinate system. The process­
ing workflow involved several stages: initial image alignment, generation of point clouds, 
construction of 3D meshes, and the development of a digital surface model. These steps 
collectively enabled the production of georeferenced orthomosaic images that can be 
seamlessly integrated with Geographic Information System (GIS), thereby enhancing

and geographically accurate representation of the surveyed area, is shown in Fig. 4.
Two distinct annotation methods were employed, each tailored to the specific require­
ments of the corresponding model types. For object detection tasks, bounding box 
annotations were created using the LabelImg tool [25], where objects of interest were 
manually enclosed within square boxes. In contrast, segmentation tasks required a more 
detailed approach; the CVAT tool [26] was used to generate precise brush masks for each 
object within the images. Four classes were defined for classification, with their char­
acteristics and visual representations outlined in Table 2. This annotation process was 
critical for enhancing the model's ability to differentiate between classes, especially in 
cases where objects exhibit overlapping or visually similar features, such as visible water, 
invisible water, and irrigated water. The dataset presented additional challenges due to 
frequent overlaps between vegetation and water bodies, as seen in marshy or vegetated 
aquatic environments. In these cases, distinguishing between water and non-water 
regions was particularly complex. The diversity and inherent challenges of the dataset,

Key characteristics of the dataset are illustrated in Fig. 6. The Blue and NIR bands 
exhibit intentionally low pixel intensity values, introducing greater complexity to the 
task of water body detection and encouraging the development of more robust mod­

5  Phase 3: Data combination and splitting
Multispectral imagery is a powerful remote sensing tool that leverages different chan­
nel combinations to extract features from the earth’s surface. Recent studies [25, 26] 
have introduced new water extraction indices such as the Flood/Water Extraction Index 
(FWEI) and Sentinel-2 Flood Mapping Index (SFMI) to improve the detection of water 
bodies and flooded areas in Sentinel-2 imagery. However, satellite sensors typically cover 
large geographical areas with moderate spatial resolution (e.g., 10 m per pixel [27]) for 
global monitoring. In contrast, UAV systems, such as the DJI Phantom 4 Multispectral,

capture images at much higher spatial resolutions (0.0265 m/pixel) over smaller areas. 
For this study, we implemented the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) due to 
its simplicity, effectiveness, and historical validation [28], as it efficiently highlights water 
features that may indicate potential mosquito larval habitats in high-resolution aerial 
imagery.
Three different types of channel combinations were used in this study, each serving 
a unique purpose by providing insights into various environmental and geographical 
phenomena: RGB + NIR: The RGB combination provides fundamental colour informa­
tion that helps distinguish between vegetation, soil, and water. The NIR band, which 
is highly reflective in vegetation but absorbed by water, enables better differentiation 
between water bodies and vegetated areas. This combination enhances the model’s abil­
ity to detect water bodies by distinguishing land and vegetation. NDWI + NIR + Green: 
NDWI is specifically designed to enhance water body detection in multispectral imag­
ery. Combining NDWI and NIR maximises the reflection of water while minimising 
vegetation reflection. Adding the Green band further improves water body detection, 
as water strongly absorbs in the Green wavelength. Red + NDWI + Blue: This combina­
tion is effective for identifying water bodies, even in areas with diverse land features. 
NDWI is tailored for detecting water, and the Red and Blue bands provide additional 
distinct water signatures. Research by Bulent Ayhan [29] indicates that a similar com­
bination (NDVI, Green, and Blue) achieved high accuracy in detecting chlorophyll-rich 
vegetation, which inspired us to explore similar spectral combinations for water body 
detection.
The NDWI index highlights open water features in satellite imagery, making water 
bodies stand out against soil and vegetation. It is calculated using the visible Green and 
Near-Infrared bands [30], with a minor constant added to the denominator to prevent 
division by zero. The equation for NDWI is defined as:

Our dataset was refined to include 880 images, each containing six spectral bands for 
training and validation. For the testing dataset, images were collected from two distinct 
areas: one like the training set and another from a completely new region around Ben 
Cat town. The distribution of the test set was kept consistent with that of the training 
set, and some unseen images from the training data were also included. This strategy 
was designed to evaluate the models using unseen data and under varying weather con­
ditions, thus testing their generalisation capabilities. The number of images in each out­
put folder is detailed in Table 1.
To ensure fair model performance across all class types, we applied a stratified k-fold 
cross-validation method to split the dataset into five folds. This method helps address 
the issue of imbalanced classes, ensuring that folds with fewer samples still contribute to 
the training and validation process. The model was trained over five iterations, with each 
fold being used for validation once while the remaining four folds were used for train­
ing. The final performance metric was averaged across these five iterations to provide a 
stable and robust evaluation of the model’s performance.

6  Phase 4: Model training
A primary objective of this study is to support the computer vision community with 
resources for detecting water bodies from multispectral imagery. This section compares 
various deep learning techniques by training and evaluating them using our dataset, 
providing a comprehensive comparison of model performance. You Only Look Once 
version 7 (YOLOv7) [31] is an advanced object detection model known for its speed 
and accuracy. It employs a trainable bag-of-freebies approach, combining mosaic aug­
mentation, self-adversarial training, and a CSPNet backbone. These strategies enhance 
the model’s robustness, generalisation, and efficiency without increasing computational 
complexity or inference time, improving performance in detecting objects in images 
or videos. Similarly, DocF, proposed by Fang Qingyun [32], maximises the potential of 
multispectral images by using a Cross-Modality Fusion Transformer. This simple yet 
powerful method differs from traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by 
leveraging Transformer architecture to capture long-distance relationships and incorpo­
rate broader contextual details during feature extraction.
DPENet [33] and CCTNet [34], proposed by Ziyi Chen and Honglin Wu, respec­
tively, both employ two main branches to improve performance by combining spatial 
and global information. DPENet uses a CNN-based branch for spatial details (e.g., edges, 
shapes) and a Swin Transformer-based branch for dividing images into non-overlapping 
windows. Self-attention blocks in DPENet generate attention vectors to capture long-
distance dependencies. CCTNet utilizes an encoder with stacked residual blocks for 
spatial information and a decoder with Transformer blocks to identify global dependen­
cies. For bounding box-based models, YOLOv7, YOLOv7x, and DocF were specifically 
tested for comparison.
In contrast, the Multispectral Semantic Segmentation Network (MSNet) [35] is a deep 
CNN model that processes multispectral bands, dividing them into visible (RGB) and 
invisible (NIR) groups. MSNet utilises ResNet-50 as a feature extractor and employs 
cascaded upsampling to increase resolution. The model fuses multi-scale image and 
spectral features through a pyramid structure and has demonstrated competitive perfor­
mance in remote sensing tasks. RTFNet, proposed by Yuxiang Sun [36], also combines 
visible and invisible spectral bands for object detection. This network uses an encoder-
decoder design with ResNet for feature extraction and a new decoder to restore the fea­
ture map resolution. Finally, U-Net [37], a traditional and powerful model for semantic 
segmentation, was also evaluated for benchmarking purposes on the multispectral UAV 
imagery dataset.
The experiments were conducted on a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) server with the 
following specifications: a 12th Gen Intel i9-12900 K CPU, 64 GB RAM, and an Nvidia 
RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB VRAM. The primary training parameters included a batch 
size of 8 for maximum memory utilisation and an initial learning rate of 1e-2. A dynamic 
linear learning rate scheduler [38] was applied, adjusting the learning rate linearly from 
the initial value to a set target based on the current epoch. This scheduler contributed to 
improved accuracy and better learning performance. The optimizer used was momen­
tum-based stochastic gradient descent [39], and the binary cross-entropy loss function 
was selected for the water body detection task. The training was conducted over 200 
epochs to ensure convergence.

To optimise training time and performance, mixed precision training [40] was 
employed, combining single-precision and half-precision floating-point numbers. This 
approach sped up training while maintaining accuracy and reducing memory consump­
tion. Hyperparameter tuning was performed throughout the experiments, though the 
high dimensionality of the training dataset and the computational demands of work­
ing with multiple spectral bands made the training process time intensive. To address 
this, the batch size was adjusted to maximize memory utilisation, and the learning rate 
scheduler dynamically adjusted the learning rate as training progressed, ensuring effi­
cient convergence while balancing computational constraints.
7  Phase 5: Model evaluation
The evaluation process involves analysing the predictions made by the models on test 
folds against the ground truth image annotations. These predictions correspond to the 
anticipated positions of the target (water bodies) within the test images. For an image I 
and a chosen threshold t, detection within I that exhibits a score surpassing the thresh­
old t is considered positive, while others are negative. In practice, prediction results by 
a computer vision model will be in one of four outcomes: True Positive, the number of 
correct positive predictions, is denoted with TP(I,t); False Positive, the number of incor­
rect positive predictions, is FP(I,t); False Negative, the number of incorrect negative 
prediction, is designated as FN(I,t); True Negative, the number of correct negative pre­
dictions, is denoted with TN(I,t). The performance of the models in identifying water 
bodies was assessed within a specific test fold, the formula was established for precision

8  Results
A comparative analysis of the training performance of various deep learning models on 
the UAV multispectral imagery dataset for detecting water bodies was evaluated with F1 
score and Dice score metrics for different spectral band combinations.
YOLOv7, with an equivalent configuration, demonstrates the most stable training pro­
cess, characterised by a smoother F1 score progression on the validation set and fewer 
oscillations during the early epochs, particularly between 0.7 and 0.8 (Fig. 7). It also con­
verges more quickly, as shown by the faster rise in F1 score during the initial stages of 
training. As a result, both YOLOv7 and YOLOv7x achieve the highest F1 scores across 
all subplots, highlighting their strong final performance. Overall, the YOLOv7 baseline 
proves to be an effective model for bounding box detection, combining stability with 
rapid convergence. In contrast, DocF requires 200 epochs to reach convergence but still 
achieves the lowest F1 score compared to YOLOv7 and YOLOv7x. This is likely due to 
its Transformer-based architecture, which typically requires a large dataset to effectively 
learn complex patterns and relationships for optimal performance.
The performance of the bounding box model on the test set for the ‘visible water’ and 
‘building’ labels, which are distinguished by their unique spectral and structural fea­
tures, is illustrated in Fig. 8. For ‘visible water,’ the true positive rates are 0.81 (YOLOv7x 
Red + NDWI + Blue) and 0.79 (DocF RGB + Green + NIR + NDWI), with minimal mis­
classification into the background (0.13 for YOLOv7x and 0.16 for DocF). For ‘build­
ing,’ the true positive rates are 0.83 and 0.84, though there is notable misclassification 
into the background (0.41 and 0.37). In contrast, the model struggles with the ‘invisi­
ble water’ and ‘irrigated water’ classes, frequently misclassifying them as background. 
‘Invisible water’ achieves true positive rates of 0.36 and 0.47, with substantial misclas­
sification into the background (0.61 and 0.47). Similarly, ‘irrigated water’ achieves true 
positive rates of 0.58 and 0.67, with misclassifications into the background at 0.42 and 
0.31. These results highlight the model’s ability to accurately identify distinct features,

9  Discussion
Low-cost UAVs equipped with multispectral cameras offer a powerful tool for captur­
ing images of small-to-medium-sized water bodies and surrounding objects in urban 
and peri-urban areas, particularly under complex tropical conditions marked by dense 
vegetation and extended rainy seasons. The 16 iterations of UAV flights, combined with 
orthomosaic image generation, object annotation, and multispectral band combination, 
have proven productive in generating a high-quality multispectral image dataset essen­
tial for effective deep learning-based water body detection. Our framework integrates 
low-cost UAV imagery with spectral indices (NIR and NDWI) and deep learning tech­
niques to enable rapid, accurate, and scalable detection of small-to-medium-sized water 
bodies. This streamlines workflows for arbovirus vector habitat mapping in tropical and 
peri-urban regions, reducing reliance on labour-intensive surveys and enhancing the 
scalability of arbovirus vector control initiatives, ultimately mitigating tropical vector-
borne disease transmission, which is influenced by climate-sensitive factors such as tem­
perature, precipitation [43], and breeding dynamics [41].
A UAV multispectral dataset for small-to-medium-sized water body detection has 
been created, comprising 982 images with five spectral bands and four aquatic classes: 
visible water, invisible water, irrigated water, and buildings. Unlike semi-automated 
Technology-Assisted Digitizing (TAD) approaches [42], our method combines manual

The integration of multispectral bands (RGB, NIR, NDWI) significantly improved 
model performance over RGB-only methods, with Dice scores increasing from 0.88 to 
0.92 in our dataset. While RGB provides basic colour differentiation [11–13], it struggles 
in dense vegetation and mixed land cover. NDWI addressed these limitations by enhanc­
ing water-boundary contrast through its sensitivity to Green and NIR wavelengths, while 
NIR’s strong reflectance contrast between water and vegetation enabled precise delinea­
tion of overlapping features. As a result, the RGB + NIR + NDWI combination enables 
accurate detection of aquatic habitats in complex tropical environments.
Our experiments demonstrate the superior performance of deep learning models 
over traditional methods in detecting aquatic habitats using UAV multispectral imag­
ery. Object segmentation models, such as U-Net and MSNet, with multispectral inputs, 
achieved robust detection accuracy and captured pixel-level details in complex tropi­
cal environments. In contrast, bounding box models like YOLOv7x balanced speed and 
precision, achieving a weighted F1 score of 0.74, making them suitable for real-time 
surveys. Multi-class detection improved generalisation by learning class-specific fea­
tures for irregular water body shapes and dense vegetation, with the weighted F1 score 
addressing class imbalances. While segmentation models require more computational 
resources, their precision in challenging tropical conditions makes them robust, whereas 
bounding box models offer efficient alternatives. The deep learning approach addresses 
the scalability and accuracy limitations in tropical arbovirus vector mapping.
However, the study’s reliance on UAV multispectral imagery from specific envi­
ronmental conditions in Vietnam introduces potential generalisability constraints, 
particularly for regions with distinct seasonal variations not represented in the data­
set. Model performance may fluctuate in unobserved scenarios, such as the transition 
from monsoon to dry seasons, where water body spectral signatures shift dramati­
cally. Additionally, the computational demands of processing multi-modal data (e.g., 
RGB + NIR + NDWI) could hinder deployment in resource-constrained settings with 
limited access to high-performance computing infrastructure.
Future work should prioritise expanding the dataset to include diverse geographies 
and seasonal cycles, which will enhance model robustness for global applicability. Devel­
oping lightweight algorithms optimised for edge computing, such as quantized neural 
networks, could reduce inference latency and hardware dependencies.
10  Conclusion
In summary, we developed a method for detecting small-to-medium-sized water bodies, 
which is crucial for mapping arbovirus vector aquatic habitats. Using a DJI Phantom 4 
Multispectral UAV, we captured images of rural and peri-urban areas in Binh Duong, 
Vietnam. Various multispectral band combinations, including RGB, NIR, and NDWI, 
were selected to enhance the spectral contrast between water bodies and surround­
ing land cover. Six state-of-the-art deep learning models—YOLOv7, YOLOv7x, DocF, 
U-Net, MSNet, and RTFNet—were evaluated. The experimental results demonstrated 
that object segmentation models, particularly U-Net and MSNet, performed exception­
ally well, with Dice scores of 0.92, in detecting small-to-medium-sized water bodies. 
These findings underscore the viability of UAV multispectral imagery and deep learning

Abstract: Vector-borne diseases pose a persistent public health challenge in tropical regions such as Vietnam, where traditional ground-based surveillance methods struggle with scale and accuracy. This study presents a framework that integrates Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) multispectral imagery with deep learning techniques to detect small-to-medium-sized water bodies, important habitats for arbovirus vectors. High-resolution multispectral images were captured with the DJI Phantom 4 (P4M) Multispectral UAV in rural and peri-urban areas of Binh Duong province in Vietnam. A curated dataset of 982 annotated images was created, comprising RGB, near-infrared (NIR), and normalized difference water index (NDWI) bands. Six state-of-the-art object detection and segmentation models were evaluated, including YOLOv7, YOLOv7x, DocF, U-Net, MSNet, and RTFNet. Among them, segmentation models (U-Net and MSNet) using RGB + Green + NIR + NDWI achieved the best performance with dice scores above 0.92. The results show that the combination of UAV multispectral imagery with deep learning significantly improves the detection accuracy of water bodies in complex tropical conditions. This approach provides a scalable, cost- effective solution for mapping small water bodies and contributes to targeted vector control and disease prevention measures in arbovirus-prone regions.
